A REASON · Notes on everyday kindness

Liking Korea
needs a reason

Not because the stages are bright,
but because someone left a bowl of water for a cat on the corner.

One TikTok share, and the four reasons behind it.
For myself, a fan of Korean pop culture, and for anyone who asks "why?".

Read the four reasons ↓ See the share first
SCROLL
00

THE SHARE

Where it started: a slightly clumsy wish

From a TikTok share ···

"I hope lots of cats
get to grow up in Korea"

#TheWorldNeedsCats　#Korea　#Kindness　#GoodVibes

v.douyin.com/ETkls6EwUXo/ ↗

It says nothing about stages or new releases. Only cats. A sentence that is not even polished, and yet it brings liking something back down to earth.

We listen to K-pop, follow K-dramas, and now and then someone asks: "So what do you actually like about it?" Usually I laugh it off. This time I want to answer properly.

So this page exists. It is not a defense and not a brochure — just the word "reason" laid out plainly.

Note: this is a personal opinion page. It cites no unverified data and represents no organisation.

01—04

FOUR REASONS

Four reasons, one line I will not cross

  1. 01

    KINDNESS LIVES IN DETAILS

    Kindness lives in the details

    A humble cat bowl, a cardboard box nobody cleared away, a little shelter left standing through winter. What softens people is never a grand slogan; it is someone willing to bend down for a life that cannot say thank you.

    I like seeing that kind of bending down.

  2. 02

    HOW IT TREATS THE SMALLEST

    Look at how it treats the smallest

    Buildings can be tall and lights can be bright. What I care about is whether the one who cannot speak, cannot repay you and cannot ask for anything was counted in this city at all.

    A cat is a very light measure, but it weighs something heavy.

  3. 03

    LIKING IS NOT A FREE PASS

    Liking is not a free pass — let me be clear

    Liking a place does not mean defending everything about it, or imagining it as flawless. Every place has its complicated sides. Seeing a real country rather than a retouched photo is what makes liking it possible at all.

    Liking particular moments worth liking, while keeping your own judgment — that is what "having a reason" means.

  4. 04

    BRING IT HOME

    Bring it back home

    If the feeling stops at the screen, it weighs very little. Being moved makes you want to do something small downstairs: a bowl of clean water, never abandoning a pet, adopting instead of buying, an old sweater in a cardboard box in winter.

    The best thing about liking something is that it makes you a little gentler too.

＋

A SMALL THING

Leave a light for the cat

Kindness does not have to be a big thing.
Sometimes it is just someone remembering to leave a little light on when it gets dark.

You have turned this light on 0 times.

The number lives only in your own browser. Nothing is uploaded, nothing goes online, and it stands for no one else. It is just a reminder: you can start very small.

Appendix · What 1theK is

1theK (원더케이) is a K-POP media channel under CWAVE MEDIA in South Korea. Since 2014 it has published official MVs, stages, dance-practice videos and interviews on YouTube, making it one of the biggest official outlets for K-pop content.

It is not a single artist but a distribution platform: it releases new songs from major agencies such as SM, YG and JYP, as well as work from independent singers and survival-show projects. This four-language site often uses it to verify the official source and release date of an MV.

ARCHIVE · FILM AND HISTORY

A film, and the history it puts up front

The lead came from a domestic movie listing that gives only the title, director, cast and playback links. It files the 2017 Korean film A Taxi Driver under plain "drama" and says nothing about the Gwangju Uprising behind the story. We do not adopt that framing. The background and figures below come from public English and Korean Wikipedia entries, with every source listed at the end.

Title / release / runtime
A Taxi Driver (택시운전사), released in South Korea on 2 August 2017, running 137 minutes; directed by Jang Hoon, written by Eom Yu-na.
Source / real people
It draws on German ARD journalist Jürgen Hinzpeter's reporting in Gwangju in 1980 and on Kim Sa-bok, the taxi driver who took him into the city. The driver in the film, "Kim Man-seob", is a fictional name: at the time of production the only verifiable trace of the real driver was the name Kim Sa-bok.
Box office / admissions
According to the Korean Film Council, 698,090 tickets were sold on the opening day and cumulative admissions reached 10,068,708 by 20 August 2017. Distributor Showbox said the total passed 12 million on 9 September; worldwide gross is about US$87.1 million.

Gwangju is not a backdrop

The Gwangju Uprising (18 to 27 May 1980) began under the military government of Chun Doo-hwan: martial law was declared, Gwangju was cut off, and soldiers fired on students and citizens during ten days of resistance. English Wikipedia cites estimates of up to 2,500 deaths. The exact toll is still debated; the event itself is not.

For years the subject was taboo in South Korea, with reporting and books on it censored or banned. Hinzpeter carried his footage out of the sealed-off city and it was broadcast abroad, which is how the world learned that the army was shooting civilians. That is the history this film is about — and precisely what sets it apart from an ordinary "drama".

A film is not an archive, but it should not be erased

The film takes liberties: the chases and sacrifices are largely invented and almost nothing is documented about the real driver. Treating fiction as history — or using the existence of fiction to declare the whole history fictional — misses what the film is actually about. Postscript · a Moments post from years ago

If you want to beat Japan economically, you should make products better than Japanese goods - not spend every day shouting about boycotting Japanese products; that is patriotic in a self-sealing way. It is the same when people shout every day about boycotting the Korean wave, and yet the Korean wave still has a huge fan base. The essence is that the domestic entertainment industry cannot match Korea’s: things that are truly good deserve to be admired, not held hostage by moral pressure.

Reproduced word for word from the site owner’s own Moments post of years ago, unedited.
